why there's no point over-analysing the rba's signals on rates
monetary policy

the confusion over a '3.5 per cent' interest rate was an exception that proves an rba rule.

there has been an enormous shift in how central banks communicate in recent years. in days gone by, central bankers' public comments were often opaque and revealed little about their forecasts. in 1987, alan greenspan, then chairman of the federal reserve, famously told a us senate committee, "if i seem unduly clear to you, you must have misunderstood what i said."

for many central banks, the approach is now at the other extreme. it has become fashionable, and regarded by many as best practice, for central banks to seek to communicate their intended actions in advance. some central banks, including the federal reserve and the european central bank, have adopted "forward guidance" while others, such as the reserve bank of new zealand and the swedish riksbank, publish their expected path for the policy rate.

the challenge is that the outlook is highly uncertain and future shocks are unpredictable. even the most thorough and well-resourced central bank does not know what it will do in future with much certainty.
